content: Travel health insurance is designed to mitigate risks and costs associated with health-related issues during travel. It may provide coverage for the following: Changes to the travel itinerary due to unforeseen circumstances. Emergency evacuation for medical reasons. Medical care, including hospitalization. Treatment for mental health conditions. Repatriation of the body in the event of death. Important Considerations for Travel Health Insurance: Insurers may require proof of immunizations and/or malaria prophylaxis as a condition for approving treatment or repatriation. Travelers should familiarize themselves with the procedures for obtaining assistance and reimbursement. A copy of the travel health insurance certificate should always be kept readily accessible and presented if requested during travel. Medical Kit and Toiletries: Travelers should carry sufficient medical supplies to meet foreseeable needs for the entire duration of the trip. Toiletries should also be packed in adequate quantities unless their availability at the destination is guaranteed. A basic medical kit may include: Adhesive tape. Antiseptic wound cleanser. Bandages. Scissors and safety pins. Emollient (lubricant) eye drops. Insect repellent and insect bite treatment. Antihistamine tablets. Nasal decongestant. Antidiarrheal medication. Antiemetics and motion sickness medication. Painkillers and antipyretics. Sterile dressings. Clinical thermometer. Sunscreen and sunburn relief. Earplugs. Tweezers. Adhesive strips for closing small wounds. Adequate supplies of condoms, contraception, and other preventive measures. Oral rehydration salts and water treatment tablets. Traveling with Animals: Travelers with animals should be aware that dogs (and in some countries, cats) must be vaccinated against rabies to cross international borders. Rabies-free countries may have additional requirements. Before traveling with an animal, it is essential to research the regulatory requirements of the destination and transit countries. During Travel: Keep the following documents readily available, with a backup digital copy stored securely in email or cloud storage: Vaccination record, if applicable. Malaria prophylaxis record, if applicable. Travel health insurance certificate or national health insurance card, as appropriate. Medical attestation for prescribed medicines, if applicable. Continue taking medications for chronic health conditions, if applicable. Avoid risky behaviors, such as: Excessive alcohol consumption. Recreational drug use. Attending unsafe events or visiting unsafe environments. Approaching animals. Engaging in unsafe sexual relationships due to the risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Violating local laws and customs. Practice road safety: Wear seat belts or helmets as applicable. Drive sober. Avoid using phones while driving. Ensure the vehicle is in good repair. Respect speed limits. Plan journeys to allow the driver to rest every two hours. Avoid driving in extreme weather conditions or on poorly maintained roads. Be mindful of food and water safety precautions. Protect yourself from extreme weather conditions, such as heat waves. After Travel: Travelers should seek medical attention upon their return if they: Experience illness during or after their return, particularly fever, persistent diarrhea, vomiting, jaundice, urinary disorders, skin disease, or anogenital infection. Received treatment for malaria while traveling. May have been exposed to an infectious disease, including STIs, during travel, regardless of whether symptoms are present. Experience a deterioration of an underlying health condition (do not wait for a regular consultation appointment). Providing health personnel with information about travel history, including pre-travel vaccinations and malaria prophylaxis taken, can be helpful. Awareness of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs): Risks: Risk depends on individual behaviors. Higher risk with unprotected sex or new partners. Some areas have antibiotic-resistant STIs. Untreated STIs can lead to serious complications. Symptoms: Symptoms may be mild or unnoticed. Prompt medical attention should be sought if concerned. Prevention: Carry an adequate supply of condoms and/or other preventive measures. Consider vaccinations against human papillomavirus (HPV) and hepatitis A and B. Avoid behaviors that increase STI risk. In cases of sexual assault, seek immediate help. Testing and Treatment: Travelers should consult a healthcare professional if they suspect exposure to or symptoms of an STI during or after travel. Further Information: For more detailed guidance, refer to resources provided by the World Health Organization (WHO) on topics such as vaccine-preventable diseases, malaria, road safety, sexual health, and tuberculosis.
